nodes.label: LandGuard AI System Architecture
nodes.rationale: Four components - React frontend, Express backend, Supabase PostgreSQL, FastAPI ML service - implementing the flow PREDICT to EXPLAIN to PRIORITIZE to ACT.

nodes.label: React Frontend
nodes.rationale: Holds the Supabase anon key and the user's JWT and never the service-role key; shipping that key to a browser would hand any visitor full read/write access to every project. The anon key is safe to expose precisely because RLS constrains it.

nodes.label: Express Backend Orchestrator
nodes.rationale: The only component that talks to both the database and the ML service: verifies the JWT, resolves role from profiles, enforces authorization, validates with Zod, builds feature snapshots, orchestrates the ML call and persists results, and never returns credentials, raw SQL errors or stack traces.

nodes.label: Supabase PostgreSQL
nodes.rationale: Stores application and historical data and enforces its own invariants; RLS protects the direct-from-client path, Supabase Auth owns auth.users and profiles extends it with application role.

nodes.label: Stateless ML Service
nodes.rationale: The FastAPI service receives a feature vector and returns numbers; it holds no database credentials and never writes to Postgres. Statelessness means the model can be retrained, redeployed or rolled back without touching application data, and a failure there degrades prediction only.

nodes.label: The Prediction Flow
nodes.rationale: Authorize, read live project data, freeze a project_feature_snapshots row, POST it to the ML service, persist prediction plus explanations plus recommendations, render, and later record the real outcome joined to the snapshot only at training time. Freezing the snapshot is what makes the rendered prediction defensible months later.

nodes.label: Failed Inference Still Writes A Row
nodes.rationale: When the ML call fails, a predictions row is written with status FAILED and NULL results so the failure is visible and countable but no number is invented. The snapshot is kept and can be re-scored once the service recovers. The UI must therefore render three states - prediction, in progress, unavailable - since one that assumes a number will show a failed inference as a healthy project.

nodes.label: Two Enforcement Layers
nodes.rationale: RLS protects the direct client to PostgREST path but is bypassed entirely by the service-role key the backend uses; backend authorization covers API traffic only. Backend authorization is therefore mandatory, with RLS as the backstop if a handler forgets a check.

nodes.label: Authorization Middleware Modules
nodes.rationale: auth.middleware.ts (requireAuth), authorize.middleware.ts (requireRole, requireProjectAccess/Read/Write) and authorization.service.ts (canAccessProject, isAssignedToProject, mirroring is_assigned_to_project() in the schema), with config/roles.ts holding the role constants so no controller re-derives a policy decision and the earlier case mismatch cannot recur.

nodes.label: Explicit Authorization Failure Modes
nodes.rationale: No profile row is 403 and never a fallback to VIEWER, because under the prototype policy VIEWER reads every project nationally so defaulting to the least role would grant national read to any valid token holder. A lookup failure is 503, not 403 - a database outage is not an authorization decision.

nodes.label: Request Pipeline Ordering
nodes.rationale: requireAuth then requireProjectAccess then validate(zod) then controller then service. Authorization precedes validation so an unauthorised request is refused without the API first reporting whether its payload was well-formed, which would turn error messages into an oracle about an inaccessible project. Collection endpoints have no project id, so read scoping happens inside the service - a forgotten filter there would leak every project in the country.

nodes.label: SIH Prototype Role Visibility Policy
nodes.rationale: VIEWER and ANALYST read nationally as a documented prototype decision, because the brief does not define what bounds 'allowed project visibility' and guessing a boundary would hard-code it into the security model. It widens read for two already read-only roles, weakens no write protection, and is replaceable by narrowing SELECT policies using the existing profiles.state / profiles.department columns.

nodes.label: Pinned JWKS Verification Mode
nodes.rationale: auto mode historically treated any JWKS failure as 'no JWKS' and fell back to HS256 - a downgrade attack, since a transient outage would move verification onto a possibly weak JWT_SECRET. The verifier now distinguishes published, definitively absent and indeterminate, failing closed on the third; algorithms are pinned per mode and the modes never share key material, foreclosing algorithm confusion.

nodes.label: Dual Supabase Key Generations
nodes.rationale: Both new (sb_publishable_ / sb_secret_) and legacy key formats are accepted with fallbacks so a project can migrate without a coordinated deploy; key format and variable name are independent, and migrating formats changes nothing about trust.

nodes.label: Live Database Verification (Phase 2.3)
nodes.rationale: backend/scripts/verify-live-db.ts runs 52 behavioural checks against the deployed schema. Behaviour rather than catalog introspection, partly because PostgREST exposes only the public schema and partly because a row in pg_policies proves a policy was created, not that it does anything. RLS evidence comes only from publishable-key clients with real ES256 sessions. Indexes and NUMERIC serialisation are explicitly out of scope.

nodes.label: The Persistent-Session Anonymous Client Trap
nodes.rationale: A reported RLS leak was really a test bug: supabase-js keeps a session on the client instance even with persistSession: false and the same object had signed test users in. The tell was that 'anonymous' saw exactly one profile row - what a VIEWER sees. The script now proves current_app_role() is NULL before drawing conclusions, because a test that fails in the direction of 'looks like a security hole' is the worst way to be wrong.

nodes.label: Live API Verification (Phase 3)
nodes.rationale: backend/tests/live/api.live.test.ts exercises all 27 endpoints over real HTTP with real ES256 sessions - 61 tests, excluded from npm test, gated on LIVE_E2E=1, with every fixture removed in afterAll. It carries the weight because every service queries through supabaseAdmin and bypasses RLS, so requireProjectAccess has no backstop.

nodes.label: Deliberate Service-Role Client Usage
nodes.rationale: Used in exactly three places: profile.service.ts (resolving the caller's role before any authorization decision exists, otherwise a chicken-and-egg with the policy deciding whether they may read their own profile), authorization.service.ts (must see assignments the caller cannot), and business services. health.service.ts is the one service using the RLS-respecting client.

nodes.label: The 22P02 Malformed-UUID Bug
nodes.rationale: GET /api/projects/not-a-uuid returned 503 because translateDbError had no case for SQLSTATE 22P02 and fell through to 'database unavailable' - wrong twice, reporting a nonexistent outage and inviting a retry that can never succeed. The in-memory fake returned null for unknown ids so no unit test could reach the path. Fixed at two layers: requireProjectAccess rejects malformed ids with 400, and translateDbError maps 22P02/22007/22003 to 400.

nodes.label: Credential Boundary Table
nodes.rationale: Anon key: frontend and backend. Service-role key and JWT_SECRET: backend only, never the frontend. The ML service holds no Supabase credentials and no database connection at all.

nodes.label: Health And Observability
nodes.rationale: GET /health returns 200 whenever the process is serving with database state in the body; the probe is a single-row, single-column read of projects bounded by 2s and deliberately avoids head:true, because with head the client discards the response body and a 'table not found' error is indistinguishable from success.
